questions.question: What is the primary assignment operator traditionally used and recommended in idiomatic R code?
questions.hint: It looks like an arrow pointing to the left.
questions.explanation: In R, '<-' is the standard, idiomatic assignment operator used to assign values to variables (e.g. x <- 10), distinguishing variable assignment from function parameter definitions.

questions.question: What is the key functional difference between print() and cat() in R?
options: print() only prints numbers while cat() only prints text
print() outputs objects with vector indexing (such as [1]) and quotes, whereas cat() concatenates and prints raw unquoted text directly without vector indexing
cat() deletes the variable from memory immediately after printing
There is no difference between print() and cat()
questions.hint: cat() stands for concatenate and print, stripping vector brackets and quotes.
questions.explanation: print() prints an object formatted with its vector index (like [1]) and string quotation marks. In contrast, cat() prints raw unquoted text directly to the console, useful for clean user messages and logs.

questions.question: How does the R interpreter handle statements starting with the hash character (#)?
options: It treats them as high-priority mathematical formulas
It ignores them entirely during execution, treating them as developer comments
It compiles them directly into Machine Learning models
It triggers a syntax error
questions.hint: Think of human-readable documentation notes in code.
questions.explanation: The '#' character begins a comment in R. Everything from '#' to the end of the line is ignored by the R interpreter, allowing developers to annotate their code for clarity and maintainability.

questions.question: In what order does R execute instructions in a standard script?
options: Bottom to top
Randomly based on CPU availability
Top to bottom, sequentially line by line
Right to left
questions.hint: Computers read code the same way humans read books.
questions.explanation: R executes code sequentially from top to bottom, line by line. Any statement that depends on an earlier variable must appear after that variable has been defined.

questions.question: What symbol can be used in R to separate multiple statements written on the exact same line?
options: Comma (,)
Semicolon (;)
Colon (:)
Ampersand (&)
questions.hint: It is also commonly used to terminate statements in languages like C and Java.
questions.explanation: A semicolon ';' allows multiple statements to be written on a single line (e.g. 'x <- 10; y <- 20; print(x + y)'). However, placing one statement per line is preferred for readability.

questions.question: What does the function round(12.567, 2) evaluate to in R?
questions.hint: The second argument specifies rounding to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: round(x, digits = 2) rounds the floating-point number 12.567 to two decimal places, rounding up the second decimal from 6 to 7 because the following digit is 7, producing 12.57.

questions.question: Which of the following will trigger a syntax or execution error in R due to case-sensitivity?
options: print('Welcome')
Print('Welcome')
sqrt(49)

cat('Welcome
')
questions.hint: R is strictly case-sensitive. All built-in base functions are lowercase.
questions.explanation: R is strictly case-sensitive. Calling 'Print()' with an uppercase 'P' causes an error: 'could not find function "Print"' because the official function is named 'print()' in lowercase.

questions.question: What is the result of evaluating 'length(c(5, 10, 15, 20))' in R?
questions.hint: length() counts the total number of items in a vector.
questions.explanation: The length() function returns the count of elements inside a vector or collection. Since c(5, 10, 15, 20) contains 4 numbers, length() returns [1] 4.

questions.question: Why is syntax like 'print(paste("Total:", 40 + 10))' useful in Data Science reporting?
options: It compiles the code into an Android APK
It combines descriptive text labels with computed values into a single human-readable message
It automatically deploys a web server
It prevents variables from using computer RAM
questions.hint: The paste() function concatenates text and dynamic numbers together.
questions.explanation: paste() concatenates character strings and numeric expressions together, making it simple to print clear diagnostic summaries (e.g., 'Total: 50') during data analysis and machine learning workflows.

questions.question: In a real-world AI/Data Science pipeline, what is the role of basic R syntax during the 'Data Cleaning and Preparation' phase?
options: To physically manufacture computer hardware
To inspect missing values, transform raw measurements, filter anomalies, and calculate baseline statistics before training Machine Learning models
To design website CSS color themes
To replace the internet connection
questions.hint: Garbage in, garbage out: clean code prepares clean inputs for algorithms.
questions.explanation: Before an AI or Machine Learning algorithm can be trained, basic R syntax and functions (like mean, sum, length, and subsetting) are used to clean, validate, filter, and structure raw data into high-quality training features.
